case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Clean Water Act permits EPA (or an authorized State) to include in NPDES permits generic, narrative prohibitions that effectively make a permittee strictly liable for downstream exceedances of water-quality standards without specifying numeric or otherwise concrete effluent limits the discharger must meet.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Clean Water Act, 33 U.S.C. § 1251 et seq., principally the NPDES permitting and enforcement framework (including §§ 1311, 1312, 1313, 1318, 1342) governing effluent limitations and water-quality-based requirements in discharge permits.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: San Francisco argues that NPDES permits must provide ascertainable, enforceable discharge limits (e.g., numeric or clearly defined water-quality-based effluent limits) rather than open-ended narrative conditions that prohibit causing or contributing to violations of receiving-water quality standards. It contends that generic ‘do not cause/ contribute’ clauses unlawfully shift the regulatory burden from the permitting authority to the permittee by making compliance depend on ambient water conditions and third-party sources beyond the permittee’s control, undermining the Clean Water Act’s structure (technology- and water-quality-based effluent limits set ex ante in permits) and due-process/fair-notice principles by exposing municipalities to enforcement without clear, measurable permit benchmarks.
case_analysis.respondent_position: EPA argues that the Clean Water Act allows (and may sometimes require) narrative or general permit conditions that ensure discharges do not lead to exceedances of applicable water-quality standards, especially where precise numeric limits are impracticable or where a narrative condition is a legitimate water-quality-based limitation and a necessary backstop to protect receiving waters. EPA maintains that such provisions are consistent with the Act’s objective to achieve water-quality standards, operate alongside other permit terms (monitoring, best practices, and technology requirements), and can be enforced when a permittee’s discharge is shown to cause or contribute to a standards exceedance.
key_precedents: Entergy Corp. v. Riverkeeper, Inc., 556 U.S. 208 (2009)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s narrowing construction—treating the “cause or contribute” clause as enforceable only on a showing of material contribution—directly answers my fair-notice concern, but it does so by relocating the statute’s ex ante standard-setting function into after-the-fact causation litigation, which strains § 1342(k)’s permit-shield premise that compliance is defined by the permit’s own terms. Justice Sotomayor is right that §§ 1311(b)(1)(C) and 1342(a)(2), together with PUD No. 1 and Arkansas v. Oklahoma, allow water-quality-based conditions when technology limits are insufficient; those cases, however, underscore that the conditions must be administrable and source-specific (e.g., minimum flow), not a free-standing ambient-outcome prohibition untethered to defined effluent limits or concrete BMP/operational duties. On a minimalist, workability-focused approach, the narrowest sound holding is to permit narrative/WQ-based requirements only when the permitting authority translates them into specific, enforceable permit terms that provide clear notice and preserve the NPDES system’s predictable compliance framework. That keeps faith with precedent without converting ambient standards into a roaming, enforcement-driven obligation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s causation-limiting construction concedes the key textual problem: the permit term itself does not supply an ex ante “effluent limitation” or concrete “condition” the discharger can comply with, but instead makes legality turn on later, ambient exceedances and after-the-fact causation litigation—an inversion of the Act’s permit-centered design and § 1342(k)’s permit-shield premise. Sections 1311(b)(1)(C) and 1342(a)(2) authorize water-quality-based requirements, but—consistent with Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s points—those requirements must be translated into definite, source-specific obligations (numeric limits, specified BMPs, or comparable administrable duties), not a free-standing ambient-outcome prohibition. Arkansas v. Oklahoma and PUD No. 1 confirm the authority to impose stricter, water-quality-driven permit terms, yet they do so through identifiable, enforceable constraints (permit denial/conditions; minimum flows), not a roaming “do not cause or contribute” clause untethered to ascertainable discharge limits. Under original public meaning and the statute’s structure, respondent’s reading risks collapsing the NPDES regime back toward ambient standard enforcement—precisely what Congress displaced—so I remain with petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s narrowing construction—enforce the “cause or contribute” clause only upon proof of material causation—squarely addresses the strict-liability worry, but it does not cure the statute’s ex ante notice problem: § 1342(k)’s permit shield presupposes that compliance is determined by meeting defined permit “limitations” and “conditions,” not by later litigation over ambient exceedances in a multi-source watershed. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, PUD No. 1 and Arkansas v. Oklahoma confirm that water-quality standards may be implemented through permits, yet only through administrable, source-specific obligations (e.g., minimum flows, BMPs, numeric or otherwise measurable limits), not a free-standing ambient-outcome prohibition that effectively shifts standard-setting from permitting to enforcement. Textually, §§ 1311(b)(1)(C) and 1342(a)(2) authorize more stringent requirements, but those must still be translated into workable “limitations” on the permittee’s discharge; otherwise the permit becomes a moving target inconsistent with the Act’s permit-centered design and practical municipal planning. I therefore remain with petitioner and would allow narrative limits only when operationalized into concrete, monitorable permit terms.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh fairly press that § 1342(k)’s permit-shield and basic due process require ex ante notice, not a “moving target” keyed to ambient conditions and third-party sources. But that objection assumes the clause operates as strict liability for the river’s condition; read, as Justice Kagan urges, as a water-quality-based effluent limitation under § 1311(b)(1)(C) enforceable only on proof the permittee’s discharge caused or materially contributed to an exceedance, it functions as a familiar narrative backstop where numeric limits are impracticable and still preserves the permit’s centrality. Justice Thomas’s reliance on EPA v. California underscores Congress’s shift away from ambient-only enforcement, yet it does not negate the statute’s express command to impose “more stringent” limits necessary to meet water-quality standards, nor our recognition in PUD No. 1 and Arkansas v. Oklahoma that permits may carry tailored water-quality conditions. Under a pragmatic, real-world lens attentive to downstream harms and the limits of numeric translation, I would uphold such clauses so long as the permit cabins discretion with monitoring/BMPs and enforcement requires a concrete causal nexus to the permittee’s discharge.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s fair-notice/permit-shield critique is the hardest point for Respondent: § 1342(k) presupposes that compliance is measured against permit terms, not an ambient “moving target.” But I do not read the “cause or contribute” narrative clause as importing strict liability for the river’s condition; read with § 1311(b)(1)(C) and § 1342(a)(2), it functions as a water-quality-based effluent limitation/permit condition enforceable only on a fact-specific showing that this discharger’s effluent actually caused or materially contributed to the exceedance. Justice Gorsuch’s worry that this relocates standard-setting to enforcement undervalues that causation is a familiar limiting principle and that the permit still supplies the operative prohibition (no discharges that cause/contribute), while numeric translation may be infeasible in mixed-source waters. PUD No. 1 and Arkansas v. Oklahoma, as Justice Sotomayor notes, confirm the Act’s accommodation of water-quality-based conditions; they support requiring tailored conditions to meet standards, and the administrability concerns are best handled by a narrowing construction rather than a categorical invalidation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s narrowing construction—treating “cause or contribute” as enforceable only upon proof of material contribution—best answers the strict-liability worry, but it does not cure the textual and structural problem that the permit itself must specify ex ante the “limitations” or “conditions” the permittee can meet to obtain § 1342(k)’s shield. Sections 1311(b)(1)(C) and 1342(a)(2) certainly allow water-quality-based requirements, as Justice Sotomayor stresses, yet our precedents (PUD No. 1; Arkansas v. Oklahoma) illustrate that those requirements must be translated into administrable, source-focused obligations (e.g., flows, BMPs, numeric or otherwise determinate effluent constraints), not an ambient-outcome prohibition that effectively shifts standard-setting to after-the-fact enforcement. Even with a causation gloss, the clause leaves regulated parties guessing what discharge level is lawful and invites precisely the case-by-case litigation Congress sought to avoid by making the permit the central instrument of compliance. For those reasons, I remain with the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh that narrative backstops are permissible only when concretized into defined duties within the permit itself.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s narrowing construction—treating the clause as enforceable only on proof that the permittee caused or materially contributed to an exceedance—directly engages our fair-notice and permit-shield concerns, but it also illustrates why the clause is problematic: it turns permit compliance into after-the-fact causation litigation rather than an ex ante, administrable benchmark set in the permit itself. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 1342(k)’s permit-shield function presupposes that the permit’s terms define what compliance requires; a free-standing ambient-outcome prohibition, even with a causation gloss, leaves the regulated entity guessing and shifts standard-setting from permitting to enforcement. PUD No. 1 and Arkansas v. Oklahoma, as Justice Sotomayor notes, do support water-quality-based conditions, but they did so through specific, ascertainable obligations (e.g., a minimum flow), reinforcing that narrative standards must be translated into concrete, discharge-focused limits or defined BMP/operational duties. On an institutionalist, workability-and-precedent approach, I would allow narrative/WQ-based terms only when the permitting authority supplies the requisite specificity ex ante, not via an untethered “cause or contribute” backstop.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s narrowing construction—treating the “cause or contribute” clause as enforceable only on a showing of material causation—meaningfully mitigates strict-liability concerns, but it still does not supply the ex ante, permit-specified benchmark the text and structure of §§ 1311 and 1342 contemplate. As the Chief Justice notes, PUD No. 1 and Arkansas v. Oklahoma approve water-quality-based permitting only when translated into administrable, source-specific obligations (e.g., minimum flows), not a free-standing ambient-outcome prohibition that effectively shifts standard-setting from the permitting authority to after-the-fact enforcement. Even under a causation gloss, compliance would turn on downstream conditions and litigation-driven attribution in mixed-source waters, which sits uneasily with § 1342(k)’s permit-shield premise that the permit itself defines what lawful compliance requires. I therefore remain with Petitioner: narrative limits may be used, but only when the permit articulates concrete discharge-focused limits or defined operational/BMP duties rather than an untethered “do not cause or contribute” backstop.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan are right to stress that §§ 1311(b)(1)(C) and 1342(a)(2), as reflected in PUD No. 1 and Arkansas v. Oklahoma, allow water-quality-based permit conditions when technology-based limits fall short. But Chief Justice Roberts’s fair-notice/permit-shield concern still carries the day for me: a standalone “do not cause or contribute” clause keyed to ambient exceedances does not specify ex ante what the permittee must do, and thus shifts the standard-setting function from permitting to enforcement in a way that is procedurally unfair and practically unadministrable in mixed-source watersheds. Even under Justice Kagan’s causation-limiting construction, the permit’s content remains indeterminate because the regulated entity cannot translate that ambient-outcome prohibition into monitorable compliance obligations without the agency first articulating source-focused limits or defined BMP duties. PUD No. 1’s minimum-flow condition underscores the permissible path—translate water-quality goals into concrete, enforceable operational requirements—rather than relying on an open-ended ambient backstop as the operative permit term.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s NPDES scheme contemplates ex ante, ascertainable “effluent limitations” and permit “conditions” that give regulated entities clear, enforceable benchmarks, see 33 U.S.C. §§ 1311(a), 1311(b)(1)(C), 1342(a). While water-quality-based limits may be required, PUD No. 1 of Jefferson County v. Washington Dep’t of Ecology treated such “limitations” as concrete compliance requirements derived from water-quality standards—not open-ended prohibitions that effectively impose strict liability for downstream exceedances driven by ambient conditions and third-party sources. Reading §§ 1311(b)(1)(C) and 1342 to authorize generic “do not cause or contribute” clauses untethered to specific discharge limits would upset the Act’s permitting structure and raise serious fair-notice and administrability concerns, so the better course is a narrow ruling requiring permits to specify measurable or otherwise defined effluent limits when the agency seeks to impose liability for exceedances. This preserves EPA’s ability to use narrative limits where necessary but insists they be translated into concrete, enforceable permit terms rather than functioning as a free-standing ambient standard.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s text makes the NPDES program a system of ex ante, permit-specified “effluent limitations,” not open-ended commands keyed to ambient receiving-water conditions. Section 1342(a)(1) authorizes permits only “upon condition that such discharge will meet” the Act’s requirements, and § 1311(b)(1)(C) requires any “limitation” needed to implement water-quality standards—language that presupposes concrete, knowable limits on the discharger rather than a generic prohibition that effectively imposes strict liability for downstream exceedances caused by multiple sources. As EPA v. California ex rel. State Water Resources Control Bd., 426 U.S. 200 (1976), explains, Congress replaced the prior backward-looking water-quality regime with a permit-based framework focused on limiting discharges from point sources, which is undermined by narrative ‘do not cause/contribute’ clauses untethered to ascertainable effluent limits. Because the statute distinguishes “effluent limitations” from “water quality standards,” permits must specify enforceable discharge limits rather than delegate to the permittee the task of guaranteeing ambient compliance.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s NPDES scheme contemplates that permits will “prescribe with specificity” the discharge obligations that are enforceable against the permittee, chiefly through “effluent limitations” set ex ante under §§ 1311 and 1342, including any water-quality-based limits required by § 1311(b)(1)(C). A generic “do not cause or contribute” clause untethered to numeric or otherwise concrete effluent limits effectively converts ambient water-quality standards under § 1313 into a strict-liability permit condition dependent on downstream conditions and third-party sources, undermining the permit-shield structure and fair-notice function that Du Pont recognized as central to the program. While narrative limits may sometimes be permissible when they are themselves workable “effluent limitations,” the Act does not authorize using open-ended narrative prohibitions to shift the permitting authority’s standard-setting burden onto the permittee and later litigate in enforcement what the permit required. Practical consequences reinforce this reading: municipalities must be able to plan and operate based on clear permit benchmarks rather than face enforcement for exceedances they cannot control.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s text and structure contemplate water-quality-based requirements in permits beyond technology-based numeric limits, including “any more stringent limitation… necessary to meet water quality standards,” 33 U.S.C. § 1311(b)(1)(C), and EPA’s broad authority to “prescribe conditions for” NPDES permits, § 1342(a)(2). Consistent with PUD No. 1 of Jefferson County v. Washington Dep’t of Ecology, 511 U.S. 700 (1994), the Act allows permit conditions tailored to assure compliance with state water-quality standards, and a narrative backstop can be a legitimate WQBEL where numeric limits are impracticable and the permit otherwise contains monitoring/BMP obligations to guide compliance. Given the CWA’s core purpose to protect receiving waters and vulnerable communities downstream, I would not read the statute to bar narrative prohibitions categorically, though enforcement must still require proof that the permittee’s discharge caused or contributed to the exceedance rather than imposing true strict liability for conditions wholly beyond its control. Arkansas v. Oklahoma, 503 U.S. 91 (1992), reinforces EPA’s discretion to set permit conditions to achieve water-quality standards, supporting EPA’s approach here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s text and structure contemplate that NPDES permits may contain water-quality-based requirements in addition to technology-based effluent limits, including where numeric limits are impracticable, because § 1311(b)(1)(C) requires “any more stringent limitation… necessary to meet water quality standards” and § 1342(a)(2) gives EPA broad discretion to “prescribe conditions” to assure compliance. Our cases recognize that state and federal permitting can tie enforceable conditions to meeting water-quality standards, see PUD No. 1 of Jefferson County v. Washington Dep’t of Ecology, 511 U.S. 700 (1994), and that EPA has substantial leeway in implementing the Act’s technical scheme, cf. Arkansas v. Oklahoma, 503 U.S. 91 (1992). But workability and fair notice counsel that such narrative terms cannot operate as a strict-liability backdoor untethered to a permittee’s discharge; they must be enforced only upon a showing that the permittee’s discharge caused or contributed to the exceedance in a legally and factually supportable way. Read that way, the Act permits narrative backstop conditions while preserving the statute’s permitting-centered design and administrability.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s NPDES scheme is built around ex ante, permit-specified “effluent limitations” and “permit conditions” that are ascertainable and enforceable, not open-ended commands that a permittee must never “cause or contribute” to ambient exceedances driven by multiple sources. See 33 U.S.C. §§ 1311, 1312, 1342; and § 1342(k)’s permit-shield promise that “[c]ompliance with a permit … shall be deemed compliance” for enforcement purposes—finality that generic narrative prohibitions erode by converting the permit into a moving target tied to downstream water conditions. Reading the statute as EPA proposes also raises fair-notice and separation-of-powers concerns by effectively delegating to after-the-fact enforcement (and juries) the task Congress assigned to permitting authorities: translating water-quality standards into concrete water-quality-based effluent limits where needed. Even if narrative limits can sometimes be lawful, the Act does not permit using them to impose de facto strict liability for downstream exceedances without specifying what the discharger itself must do to comply.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s NPDES scheme is structured around ex ante, permit-specified “effluent limitations” and other concrete conditions that are administrable and provide fair notice, see 33 U.S.C. §§ 1311, 1312, 1342, with enforcement turning on whether those permit terms were met. A generic “do not cause or contribute to exceedances of water-quality standards” clause, untethered to discernible effluent limits, risks converting the permit into a roving mandate keyed to ambient conditions and third-party sources, undermining the Act’s permit-shield and workability as a predictable compliance regime. Although PUD No. 1 and Arkansas v. Oklahoma recognize broad authority to impose water-quality-based conditions, they involved specific, ascertainable limitations (e.g., a minimum streamflow requirement) rather than an open-ended narrative prohibition that functions as strict liability for downstream exceedances. Consistent with precedent, history, and practical administrability, the better reading is that § 1311(b)(1)(C) and § 1342(a)(2) allow narrative limits when necessary, but they must be translated into concrete, enforceable permit requirements rather than a generic ban on contributing to any standards exceedance.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s NPDES scheme is built around “effluent limitations” and other concrete permit “conditions” set ex ante, see 33 U.S.C. §§ 1311, 1342, with § 1311(b)(1)(C) requiring limitations “necessary to meet water quality standards”—a term that, in ordinary public meaning, connotes enforceable constraints on the discharger’s own effluent rather than an open-ended prohibition keyed to downstream ambient conditions. A generic “do not cause or contribute” clause that functions as strict liability for any receiving-water exceedance (including from third-party sources) departs from that text and undermines the permit-shield structure of § 1342(k), which presupposes that the permit itself specifies what compliance requires. PUD No. 1 supports the use of water-quality-based conditions but did so through a specific, measurable limitation (a numerical flow condition), reinforcing that water-quality protections must be translated into concrete limits rather than left as a roving narrative standard. While EPA has discretion to set permit conditions, § 1342(a)(2) cannot be read to authorize conditions that effectively replace effluent limits with indeterminate, ambient-outcome prohibitions.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Clean Water Act’s NPDES scheme is built around ex ante, source-specific “effluent limitations” and water-quality-based limits that are ascertainable and enforceable, see 33 U.S.C. §§ 1311(b)(1)(C), 1312, 1342, together with monitoring and reporting to make compliance administrable. A generic “do not cause or contribute” prohibition that turns compliance on ambient, downstream water conditions—often affected by third parties and nonpoint sources—functions as a de facto strict-liability regime untethered to any concrete discharge limit and undermines the permit shield’s core promise of fair notice and predictable compliance under § 1342(k). While EPA may use narrative limits when numeric limits are impracticable, those conditions still must describe with sufficient specificity what the permittee must do or what discharge quality it must meet, rather than shifting the burden to the permittee to ensure overall receiving-water compliance. Given the practical consequences for municipal systems and the procedural-fairness concern of enforceability without clear benchmarks, I would reverse the Ninth Circuit’s approval of open-ended receiving-water prohibitions as standalone permit terms.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Clean Water Act authorizes EPA (or an authorized State) to include generic, narrative NPDES permit prohibitions that effectively make a permittee liable for downstream exceedances of water-quality standards without specifying objective, numeric effluent limits the discharge must meet.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Clean Water Act, 33 U.S.C. § 1251 et seq., particularly the NPDES permitting framework under 33 U.S.C. § 1342 and the water-quality-based effluent limitation requirements under 33 U.S.C. § 1311(b)(1)(C) (and related water quality standards provisions generally implemented through § 1313).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: San Francisco argues that the Clean Water Act’s NPDES system requires permits to contain clear, enforceable effluent limits (or other objectively ascertainable requirements) that tell the permittee what it must do to comply, and that EPA cannot substitute open-ended, generic prohibitions that expose permittees to enforcement whenever receiving waters exceed water quality standards—especially where multiple sources contribute and the permit does not identify specific discharge limits or compliance metrics tied to the permittee’s effluent. In San Francisco’s view, such narrative “end-result” conditions undermine fair notice, convert permits into broad liability triggers rather than compliance tools, and depart from the CWA structure that channels water-quality goals into concrete permit limits and measurable obligations.
case_analysis.respondent_position: EPA maintains that the Clean Water Act allows (and sometimes requires) NPDES permits to include narrative, water-quality-based conditions ensuring discharges do not cause or contribute to violations of applicable water quality standards, including where numeric effluent limits are infeasible or cannot be reasonably derived. EPA’s position is that such conditions are a longstanding, lawful mechanism to implement § 1311(b)(1)(C)’s requirement that permits include any limitations necessary to meet water quality standards, and that they operate alongside (not in place of) other permit controls; enforcement can properly turn on whether the discharge causes or contributes to exceedances even if the permit does not specify a single numeric effluent cap for every possible pollutant/condition.
key_precedents: Entergy Corp. v. Riverkeeper, Inc., 556 U.S. 208 (2009)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas press the strongest point: a bare “cause or contribute” clause keyed to downstream exceedances risks defeating § 1342(k)’s permit-shield function because it is not, by itself, an administrable restriction on the permittee’s own discharge as contemplated by § 1362(11). But that structural concern does not justify a categorical rule, because § 1311(b)(1)(C)’s command for “any more stringent limitation … necessary to meet” WQS and § 1342(a)(2)’s authority to “prescribe conditions” plausibly authorize non-numeric, discharge-tethered permit terms when numeric translation is infeasible—exactly the middle path Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan describe. Arkansas v. Oklahoma and PUD No. 1 do not validate free-floating ambient strict liability; they support only enforceable, reviewable WQS-implementing conditions, which is why the proper minimalist course is to uphold that limited authority while making clear that an untethered, mechanism-free ambient exceedance prohibition would present serious fair-notice and permit-shield problems in an as-applied posture. Under that narrowing construction, the Petitioners’ best textual-structural objection is answered without rewriting the statute into a numeric-only regime.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s narrowing construction—permitting narrative limits if “tethered” to the discharge and paired with monitoring—concedes the central textual-structural point: the permit must itself supply ascertainable, enforceable constraints on the permittee’s discharge so that § 1342(k)’s shield can function as written. Their reliance on § 1311(b)(1)(C) (“any more stringent limitation”) and § 1342(a)(2) (“conditions”) shows only that additional permit terms are possible; it does not authorize converting ambient water-quality standards into an end-result prohibition (“cause or contribute”) that makes compliance depend on downstream exceedances driven by multiple actors and natural conditions, rather than on limits stated in the permit. Arkansas v. Oklahoma and PUD No. 1, as Justice Gorsuch observes, involved concrete, reviewable permit terms tied to the permittee’s conduct; they do not support a free-floating ambient-liability trigger that collapses the statutory distinction between effluent limits and ambient standards. Because the Respondents’ position still allows indeterminate obligations inconsistent with § 1362(11)’s discharge-focused definition and the statute’s fair-notice/permit-shield design, I remain with the Petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch put their finger on the core structural concern: § 1362(11) and § 1342(k) presuppose determinate, discharge-focused obligations, and a bare ambient “cause or contribute” clause risks collapsing that architecture into downstream strict liability. But Chief Justice Roberts’s narrowing construction, echoed by Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett, answers that objection on textualist grounds by anchoring authority in § 1311(b)(1)(C)’s broader command (“any more stringent limitation”) and § 1342(a)(2)’s separate authorization to prescribe permit “conditions” to assure compliance—while insisting the permit itself supply administrable, permit-specified mechanisms tethered to the permittee’s discharge. Arkansas v. Oklahoma and PUD No. 1 matter here because, as Roberts notes, they confirm WQS implementation through enforceable permit conditions beyond classic end-of-pipe numbers; they do not require a numeric-only rule, but they do underscore the need for concrete, reviewable terms. On that limited reading, the petitioners’ fair-notice and permit-shield concerns are addressed by demanding specificity and by leaving genuinely indeterminate drafting to as-applied challenges rather than adopting a categorical prohibition that the statute’s broader “limitations” and “conditions” language does not compel.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas press the strongest point: § 1362(11) and the § 1342(k) permit-shield architecture assume determinate, discharge-focused obligations, and a bare “cause or contribute” clause keyed to ambient exceedances risks unfair notice and multi-source attribution problems. But Chief Justice Roberts’s narrowing construction persuasively answers that structural concern without adopting a numeric-only rule that would, in practice, leave downstream communities unprotected where numeric translation is infeasible: § 1311(b)(1)(C) and § 1342(a)(2) authorize “limitations” and “conditions” beyond classic numbers so long as they are tethered to the permittee’s discharge and operationalized with concrete monitoring/implementation mechanisms. Arkansas v. Oklahoma and PUD No. 1, as Justice Kagan notes, confirm that WQS implementation can occur through enforceable permit terms beyond end-of-pipe caps; they do not authorize roving ambient strict liability, which is why the limiting construction must insist on administrability and a clear causal nexus. On my pragmatic approach, the remedy for fair-notice concerns is demanding specificity and reviewable compliance pathways, not stripping the agency of a tool that can be essential for preventing cumulative harms to vulnerable downstream users.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is the statutory-structural one: § 1362(11)’s quantitative definition and § 1342(k)’s permit-shield function make it hard to accept a permit term that effectively turns on downstream ambient exceedances attributable to multiple actors. But that critique goes to an unbounded “cause or contribute” clause, not to EPA’s authority to implement § 1311(b)(1)(C)’s “any more stringent limitation” and § 1342(a)(2)’s power to prescribe enforceable permit “conditions” where numeric translation is infeasible—text that, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, is broader than the defined term “effluent limitation.” Arkansas v. Oklahoma and PUD No. 1 cut against a categorical numeric-only rule and support a middle path: WQS may be implemented through concrete, reviewable discharge-tethered conditions (monitoring, BMPs, load allocations, trigger/response obligations), while a free-floating ambient end-result prohibition remains unlawful or at least vulnerable as applied. On pragmatic textualist grounds, I would adopt Roberts’s narrowing construction to preserve fair notice and the permit shield without reading § 1311(b)(1)(C) out of the permitting scheme.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s narrowing construction correctly recognizes that §§ 1311(b)(1)(C) and 1342(a)(2) can support some non-numeric, discharge-tethered permit terms when numeric translation is genuinely infeasible. But that concession does not save this permit condition: a bare “cause or contribute” prohibition keyed to downstream ambient exceedances still fails to impose an ascertainable, discharge-focused obligation consistent with § 1362(11)’s definition and the permit-shield design of § 1342(k), which presuppose determinate ex ante duties rather than liability that turns on multi-source ambient conditions. The precedents Roberts and Kagan invoke—Arkansas v. Oklahoma and PUD No. 1—do not undermine this conclusion because they upheld concrete, reviewable constraints (specified limits/flows/implementation measures) rather than a free-floating ambient end-result mandate. Under a textual and structural reading, EPA may require WQS-based restrictions, but it must translate them into administrable permit terms that regulate what this permittee does, not simply forbid contributing to a downstream exceedance.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s middle-path narrowing construction is the strongest argument for the Respondent, because it tries to preserve § 1342(k) fair notice by requiring narrative terms be “tethered” to the discharge and operationalized with concrete monitoring/implementation obligations. But that move essentially concedes the core problem here: the standalone “cause or contribute” clause—keyed to downstream ambient exceedances in a multi-source system—is not itself an administrable limitation on the permittee’s “quantities, rates, and concentrations” and thus cannot do the work § 1311(b)(1)(C) demands without EPA translating WQS into ascertainable permit terms. Arkansas v. Oklahoma and PUD No. 1 (invoked by Roberts/Barrett) cut against a categorical numeric-only rule, but they also support my narrower point that WQS must be implemented through specific, reviewable permit conditions rather than a free-floating ambient-liability trigger. Under an institutionalist, structure-and-workability approach, I would reverse on the ground that this kind of generalized ambient-prohibition term defeats the permit-shield’s premise of ex ante knowability and invites unpredictable enforcement.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas press the best objection: § 1362(11)’s discharge-focused definition and § 1342(k)’s permit-shield logic resist any regime where compliance turns on downstream ambient exceedances attributable to multiple sources, because that undermines determinacy and fair notice. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that the relevant operative commands here are not limited to the defined term “effluent limitation”: § 1311(b)(1)(C) requires “any more stringent limitation” necessary to meet WQS, and § 1342(a)(2) authorizes EPA to prescribe permit “conditions” to assure compliance—text that, in ordinary meaning and structure, can encompass non-numeric, narrative conditions when numeric translation is infeasible. Arkansas v. Oklahoma and PUD No. 1 do not license free-floating ambient strict liability; they support a limiting construction under which any WQS-based narrative term must be tethered to the permittee’s discharge and operationalized in administrable, reviewable requirements, with indeterminate “cause or contribute” language vulnerable as applied. On that cabined reading, the statutory architecture and the permit shield are preserved, so I do not see a textual basis for Petitioners’ categorical bar.

Oklahoma and PUD No. 1 strengthen, rather than weaken, that middle path because they approve WQS implementation through concrete, reviewable permit constraints—not a free-floating ambient end-result mandate—and thus support a limiting construction that preserves fair notice and the permit shield through specificity and as-applied review. On my procedural-fairness, pragmatic approach, the remedy for indeterminacy is to police drafting and enforcement, not to impose a categorical numeric-only rule that could disable WQS protection where numbers are not feasible.

Oklahoma, 503 U.S. 91, 105 (1992)), supporting EPA’s discretion to include water-quality-based narrative terms alongside other controls. Given the Act’s structure and precedent recognizing robust agency/state authority to prevent WQS violations, I would uphold EPA’s authority to use narrative conditions alongside other controls.
